transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-04-07
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Olivia Chen (Pioneer - Head of Platform), Marcus Lee (Pioneer - VP Eng), Dana Price (Pioneer - Security), Evan Brooks (Pioneer - SRE)

Summary (auto): discovery call. Topics: reliability, incident tolerance, fallbacks, multi-region routing, SLA expectations, Dedicated vs Private.

00:00 Maya Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll do a quick intros and then dive into how redwood handles reliability and incident tolerance for low latency APIs
00:18 Olivia Chen: thanks Maya yes quick intros on our side, I'm Olivia, head of platform for Pioneer, Marcus is our vp eng, Dana looks after security, Evan is our s re -- s r e. We're evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for a quoting service that needs 99.95% availability
00:35 Marcus Lee: yeah hi all, high throughput & low tail latency are our biggest concerns, we have about 150 qps average, peeks to ~1.6k during morning renewals, and the 95/99 latency matters to business ops
00:48 Diego Ruiz: thanks Marcus, Diego from redwood, i run infra engagements - we'll talk about routing, fallback policies, cache behavior, and what to expect from Dedicated and Private options
01:05 Dana Price: quick sec, on compliance we need audit logs, KMS integration, and SOC2 type II attestation - what's the baseline for hosted?
01:18 Maya Patel: good question, hosted includes SOC2 and bank-grade encryption at rest, we can ship audit logs to your SIEM, for Private you manage KMS and we support HSM/KMS integrations, we'll share the security slide deck after this call
01:40 Evan Brooks: also curious about data residency, can you pin regions and ensure traffic never leaves EMEA for certain tenants?
01:50 Diego Ruiz: yes, routing policies can be region pinned; we support per-tenant routing and you can restrict egress to region. For Dedicated we can provision capacity in your chosen region or multi region if needed.
02:10 Marcus Lee: ok can you explain multi-region failover? specifically how requests get routed during an outage and how session/kv cache is handled?
02:25 Diego Ruiz: sure, we typically use active-active across two regions for latency sensitive workloads. On failure we have automated routing policies - requests shift to the healthy region; there's an optional global load balancer or we integrate with your LB. KV cache and prefix caching are per region - so in a failover you will see cold-cache penalties. We also offer a cross-region async cache warmup to reduce tail impact but it's eventual consistency
03:05 Olivia Chen: "K V cash" in transcript - is that the same as our in-memory prefix cache? we do a lot of reuse across sessions
03:12 Diego Ruiz: yes, it's the prefix/K V cache that stores KV for transformer decoding; cold-starts can add 50-200ms depending on model and sequence length. We can mitigate via prewarming and by routing a percentage of traffic to the backup region before failure (canary mirroring)
03:40 Marcus Lee: how about model fallbacks - if a high-performance model becomes unavailable or overloaded, do you do auto-fallback to a cheaper/quantized variant? and what's the impact on latency/quality?
03:55 Maya Patel: correct - Robertson (sic) - sorry redwood supports model variants and automatic fallback rules. You can configure by policy: latency-first, cost-first, or quality-first. Fallbacks to a quantized variant reduce memory and cost but may change output slightly. We recommend A/B checking on critical prompts during pilot
04:20 Dana Price: on the security side, during failover we need to maintain audit continuity - can logs and request IDs be forwarded/merged across regions? we use strict tamper-evident logging
04:35 Diego Ruiz: yes we emit correlated request IDs and we can centralize logs to your SIEM; we also provide immutable audit events for control-plane ops. For Private deployments, logs live in your VPC/on-prem by default
05:02 Marcus Lee: SLA expectations: our legal team wants at least 99.9% uptime for inference endpoints and a 99th percentile tail under 300ms for core endpoints, is that achievable?
05:22 Maya Patel: for Hosted we publish SLOs at the account level - 99.9% is in the enterprise SLA for Dedicated; tail latency depends on model and config. We should run a benchmark with your critical prompts and target model; in pilot we'll instrument token-level latency and KV cache hit rates to tune batching and quantization profiles
06:05 Olivia Chen: what's the typical mitigation during capacity constrained events? like a GPU node failure in region - do you spill to another model or region, and what's the automation?
06:20 Diego Ruiz: multiple layers: 1) autoscaling within Dedicated pools; 2) automated routing to other regions/pools based on policy; 3) model variant fallback if region capacity tight; plus soft-degradation where we reduce max-generation length or change batching strategy to preserve throughput. All of this is configurable per-route
06:51 Evan Brooks: in practice, do you do throttling per customer to protect noisy neighbors? and what about token-based rate limits?
07:05 Maya Patel: yes rate limits and token quotas are first-class. We also have burst buckets and can apply per-route QoS. For Dedicated you get isolation via reserved GPU pools so noisy neighbor risk is much lower
07:25 Marcus Lee: can we do canary/failsafe routing? e.g., route 95% production to primary region and 5% to backup for warm cache and to test fallback health?
07:40 Diego Ruiz: absolutely, that's a common pattern - percent-based routing and canary mirroring, plus automatic promotion if health checks pass. We can tie that to traffic shaping policies in the console
08:05 Olivia Chen: about data egress, we have strict egress controls - can you provide detailed network topology diagrams for Dedicated and Private? also does hosted require egress to redwood control plane from our VPC?
08:20 Maya Patel: hosted uses a managed control plane but we can restrict egress endpoints and provide IP allowlists. For Private, control plane can be customer-managed - minimal or zero egress depending on deployment. We'll attach the topology diagram in the follow-up
08:50 Marcus Lee: let's talk incidents - what's the incident lifecycle? page, escalation, post-mortems, and how are rolling back of model versions handled?
09:05 Diego Ruiz: our incident process: pager escalation, ops runbooks, automated rollback of latest model routing if quality/latency regressions detected. Rollbacks are route-level; for Dedicated we can also do canary rollouts with automatic rollback on SLI breaches. Post-mortems are shared with customers for enterprise contracts
09:35 Olivia Chen: who owns the runbooks for a Private on-prem install? we want to avoid vendor lock-in and be able to run critical ops ourselves
09:44 Diego Ruiz: for Private, you own the runtime and ops; Redwood provides the control-plane tools, documentation, and optional support runbooks. We also offer a managed on-call add-on if you want Redwood to handle 24/7 ops
10:12 Marcus Lee: side question: how does model compilation/kernel selection affect failover? like if a model is compiled for one GPU type and fallback region has different hardware, is switching seamless?
10:30 Diego Ruiz: we maintain compatible model variants per hardware type; the runtime can route to a compatible compiled artifact. In some cases there is a small cold-start due to re-compilation, but we try to keep binary compatible variants for common hardware profiles. We'll map your chosen regions' hardware during pilot
11:05 Evan Brooks: example scenario: primary region loses one rack; autoscaler can't recover fast enough; what's expected RTO and what we can do to improve it?
11:20 Diego Ruiz: RTO depends on capacity headroom and pre-provisioned burst. If you preprovision spare nodes in the secondary region or have burst capacity, failover can be under a minute for routing with degraded latency; without headroom, we might start throttling or fall back to a lower-latency model variant while routing takes place. We recommend baseline capacity planning during pilot
12:00 Olivia Chen: is there any way to keep KV/prefix cache warm across regions to avoid cold penalty? you mentioned async warmup - can you elaborate?
12:12 Diego Ruiz: options: 1) canary mirroring where a small percentage of production traffic is mirrored to backup region to populate cache, 2) proactive prewarm jobs based on recent traffic patterns, 3) hybrid approaches using shared persistent cache (adds complexity and eventual consistency). We usually start with mirror + prewarm for simpler maintenance
12:50 Marcus Lee: cost question - running active-active across two regions obviously doubles infra cost, how do you recommend balancing cost vs SLA?
13:05 Maya Patel: common pattern: active-passive with warm standby for cost savings, or active-active for highest availability. Also model quantization, batching, and cache tuning reduce per-token cost. Redwood Optimize can suggest profiles for your workload after we ingest trace samples
13:40 Dana Price: audit & compliance again - do you sign BAA for PHI, and do you support SC and SAML for SSO?
13:55 Maya Patel: we do BAA for specific enterprise contracts, and we support SAML/SCIM for SSO and RBAC across the console. For Private we integrate with your IdP directly
14:20 Evan Brooks: in a failover where region B takes traffic, how do we keep request ordering or session affinity for stateful flows?
14:30 Diego Ruiz: we recommend stateless APIs for inference; for session affinity we can use sticky routing at LB layer or store minimal session state in a global datastore. Redwood's runtime is stateless by design, so ordering is handled client-side or with external session stores
15:00 Marcus Lee: sample telemetry - what do you provide out of the box? token-level latency, per-route error rates, model variant usage?
15:15 Maya Patel: yes dashboards include token-level cost, latency percentiles, per-route model usage, error traces, and retention windows. For Dedicated we can extend retention and give you raw traces for in-house analysis
16:00 Olivia Chen: ok a quick scenario test: we need to guarantee quote response under 300ms 99th pctl for core endpoints. Will Dedicated get us there with right hardware?
16:16 Diego Ruiz: likely yes - with tuned models, local KV hits, and right GPU class we can meet 300ms 99th for short prompts. We'll need your prompt set to benchmark. Our recommended pilot uses the exact production prompts to validate
17:00 Marcus Lee: timeline and procurement - if pilot goes well who signs the order? procurement/legal will want standard terms and liability caps, and we need pricing for Dedicated reserved capacity vs private perpetual license
17:18 Maya Patel: we'll send a pricing sheet: Hosted metered, Dedicated reserved (monthly commit tiers), Private enterprise (platform + support). Legal typically negotiates SLA credits and liability caps - we can introduce our legal point of contact when you want to proceed
18:00 Olivia Chen: one more on live failures - do you have a runbook that outlines automated vs manual steps and how escalations occur? we need to map to our internal SOC playbooks
18:14 Diego Ruiz: yes, we have runbooks per failure class (hardware, control-plane, model quality). We'll share a sanitized runbook and can work with your SREs to align escalation policies
19:00 Marcus Lee: ok let's talk pilot specifics - two regions, Dedicated, one model family, 2-week run, and we will provide prompt set + traffic replay; is that feasible to start Apr 20?
19:18 Maya Patel: yes that's feasible - Diego will scope infra and we'll send a formal pilot plan. Pilot success criteria: meet 99.9% availability for the endpoints in pilot window, 99th < 350ms, and fallback test where we simulate regional outage with warm standby
20:05 Olivia Chen: any questions from Redwood on our end that we haven't covered?
20:12 Diego Ruiz: one ask: can you share traffic percentile CSV and a small sample of critical prompts after the call? that'll help with kernel selection and batching tuning
20:28 Olivia Chen: yes we'll prepare and get that over by Friday
20:35 Maya Patel: perfect. One last note: competitors - you mentioned considering Anthropic and some self-hosted infra; the differentiator we aim for is operational controls and predictable cost during incidents
20:55 Marcus Lee: appreciate that.
21:05 Dana Price: ok we need the security slide deck and SOC2 report, please send to security@pioneerinsurance.com
21:12 Maya Patel: will do.
21:20 Olivia Chen: recap and next steps?
21:24 Maya Patel: recap - send SLA/fallback/security docs, Diego to schedule technical deep dive week of Apr 13, pilot proposal for Apr 20 two-region Dedicated, customer to share prompts/traffic and network constraints. Action items assigned.
21:45 Marcus Lee: sounds good thanks everyone
21:50 Diego Ruiz: thanks all, talk soon
22:00 Call ends

Notes: occasional transcription issues (product names and acronyms sometimes mis-typed). References to attached artifacts: "security slide deck", "pilot plan", "pricing sheet", and "topology diagram" - these will be circulated post-call as links.
